title: Epic of Gilgamesh (Old Babylonian version)
summary: The Epic of Gilgamesh, a Mesopotamian poem in cuneiform, survives in Old Babylonian tablets dated about 1800 BCE, including a fragment recounting how Shamkat persuades Enkidu to go to Uruk. By the end of the second millennium BCE it was an 11-tablet text, and a 12th was added in the eighth century BCE.

uncertainty.note: Sulaymaniyah tablet T-7544 is dated circa 1800 BCE on the middle chronology; Dalley dates the Nineveh fragments only to the Old Babylonian period.

as_recorded.value: Circa 1800 BCE; approximately 1800 BCE (middle chronology), around the reign of Rim-Sin of Larsa
fragments date to the Old Babylonian period (BM 134537 A–I and 134538, Nineveh)

where.modern_name: Uruk (Warka), Al-Muthanna Governorate, Iraq (setting of the story; the place of composition is not established)
where.historical_name: Babylonia, southern Mesopotamia (Uruk is where the story is set; no composition place is named in the sources)

importance.justification: The sources treat it as a long-lived text that grew to 11 and then 12 tablets over about a millennium.

The provenance of the c. 1800 BCE tablet is unknown; the Uruk pin is the story setting with 300 km uncertainty, not a sourced composition site. The 11-then-12-tablet statement comes from the Biblical Archaeology Society page about a later copy.
